{"id": "12:36/q34", "question": "What specific acts made Joseph known as beneficent in prison?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q34/p1", "position": "He cared for sick and distressed inmates, aided the needy, made space, urged patience and worshipped God.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak adds practical aid and intercession; Qatada adds hope of reward, cleansing and devotion; al-Mawardi lists accepting excuses and putting others first; Ibn Kathir adds honesty and trustworthiness. {"id": "12:36/q36", "question": "What lesson does Joseph's response give about teaching?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q36/p1", "position": "A teacher may give essential counsel before answering and mention expertise to guide listeners toward God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi draws this from Joseph's preaching and claim to know interpretations; al-Tabrisi links the address to wisdom in 16:125."}]}
{"id": "12:36/q37", "question": "What did Joseph mean by promising to interpret before food arrived?", "turns_on": "Whether the coming food is dream material or ordinary provision.", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q37/p1", "position": "He claimed prophetic foreknowledge of the prisoners' food dreams.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi says most commentators take the promise this way."}, {"id": "12:36/q37/p2", "position": "He meant ordinary waking food: what it was, when and how much they ate.", "reasons": "The prisoners suspected divination, but Joseph attributed the knowledge to God. {"id": "12:36/q39", "question": "What does the verse establish about dreams and their interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether any dream can disclose reality, and which causes distinguish truthful from ordinary dreams.", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q39/p1", "position": "Some dreams truly disclose future or hidden events and can be interpreted.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj says denying all true dreams contradicts scripture and a prophetic report of one-fortieth of prophecy. Al-Razi cites a report of one forty-sixth and explains the soul's sleep-time access to higher realities. Al-Tabataba'i argues correspondence to future events is not chance and distinguishes bodily and emotional dreams from sound dreams."}, {"id": "12:36/q39/p2", "position": "Dreams include self-talk, satanic dreams and true dreams; many arise from bodily, emotional or chance causes.", "reasons": "Al-Razi accepts the prophetic threefold report as rationally sound. Al-Tabataba'i says imagination recombines sensory images, affected by body, temperament and emotions; all dreams have causes, though many do not foretell external events. He grants naturalists' account for some dreams."}, {"id": "12:36/q39/p3", "position": "All dreams are unreal.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i rejects this inference from ordinary bodily and emotional causes; he says some dreams relate to external truth."}]}
{"id": "12:36/q40", "question": "How can a true dream disclose reality, and when does it need interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether the perception is direct or mediated by symbolic transformations.", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q40/p1", "position": "The sleeping soul can reach nonphysical causes, seeing them directly or as symbolic images.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says bodily distraction lessens in sleep. Al-Tabataba'i distinguishes physical, imaginal and intellectual worlds; a sound soul may perceive causes clearly, while symbols or opposites such as crown/honor and darkness/ignorance need return to their meanings. Tangled symbolic chains resist interpretation. Ibn Sirin's Ramadan caller example illustrates decoding."}, {"id": "12:36/q40/p2", "position": "Some dreams are clear without symbolic interpretation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i says clear dreams may reveal events directly and identifies these apart from interpretable symbols."}]}
{"id": "12:36/q41", "question": "What do reports say about falsely claiming a dream?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q41/p1", "position": "A dream liar will be ordered on Judgment Day to tie grains together, an impossible task.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's version says two barley grains; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan sahih. ʿAli's version says a grain and is graded hasan. Al-Thaʿlabi's accompanying report also warns that secret eavesdroppers receive molten lead in the ear."}]}
{"id": "12:36/q42", "question": "How does this prison scene connect with later events and the sura's design?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q42/p1", "position": "Dream interpretation in prison eventually leads to Joseph's release and rule.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says divine grace made both his interpretive skill and kindness means of rescue; Qushayri says companionship bore fruit when the forgetful cellmate later spoke at 12:46; Islahi links the correct interpretations to the king's dream and appointment."}, {"id": "12:36/q42/p2", "position": "The prison's apparent humiliation became honor under God's direction of events.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi cites al-Razi on gentleness mingled with trial and sees the prison fulfilling a prior promise. {"id": "12:36/q43", "question": "What inward meanings are given to the two dreamers and their visions?", "turns_on": "The two symbolic roles and dream images differ.", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q43/p1", "position": "The cupbearer represents spiritual love pressing love's wine from heart-knowledge while witnessing sleeps.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani gives this symbolic reading."}, {"id": "12:36/q43/p2", "position": "The baker represents soul-desire pursuing pleasure, with birds rushing toward gratification.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani connects bread with sustenance of the soul and the birds' quick movement with appetites."}]}
{"id": "12:36/q44", "question": "How is the next verse's repeated mention of Hereafter disbelief parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the repeated element functions as emphasis or syntactic resumption.", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q44/p1", "position": "The repetition emphasizes their disbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi reports this grammatical analysis."}, {"id": "12:36/q44/p2", "position": "The first pronoun is redundant and the second clause supplies the sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi compares another Quranic construction with a first clause treated as omitted and a new clause begun."}]}

{"id": "12:36/q53", "question": "Why is the verb 'entered' singular before 'two youths'?", "turns_on": "Whether a preceding verb receives number agreement from a delayed subject in the dialect being used.", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q53/p1", "position": "A verb before its delayed dual subject normally remains singular.", "reasons": "Sībawayh explains that a preceding verb does not take a dual or plural suffix before its following subject; the noun itself supplies the number. {"id": "12:36/q54", "question": "What sources did interpreters use for dreams beyond Quranic examples?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:36/q54/p1", "position": "They drew on Joseph's dreams and the prisoners' visions, then explanatory Sunnah, sayings, proverbs and customary usage for unresolved cases.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī reports this sequence and relates customary usage to the command to observe recognized practice."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q01", "question": "Why does Joseph again call them his prison companions?", "turns_on": "Which rhetorical effect of the renewed address is emphasized.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q01/p1", "position": "The address renews their attention and marks the importance of his answer.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says Joseph returns to their interpretation after the more important teaching about religion; al-Alusi says interpretation is a new topic after his proof of knowledge; Ibn Ashur says the vocative stresses the interpretation."}, {"id": "12:41/q01/p2", "position": "The address invokes shared hardship and friendship.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says shared imprisonment removes worldly pretension and softens the heart."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q02", "question": "Which prisoner receives each predicted fate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q02/p1", "position": "The cupbearer returns to royal wine service, and the baker is crucified and eaten by birds.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Thalabi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi, and others specify three more prison days; some say release and crucifixion occur on the fourth. The cupbearer dreamed of grapes or a vine, the baker of bread baskets and birds. Ibn Ishaq, Mujahid and later reports name them variously Nabu, Nabwa or Banu, and Mujlith, Majlatha, Majlath, Malhab or Mujlab; the name forms vary. Al-Mawardi calls the condemned man the king's baker; the Imami report calls both king's servants. Study Quran says the baker's head is eaten after death and for his crime."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q03", "question": "Why are the two prisoners not named in the prediction?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse reproduces Joseph's veiled speech or condenses a more explicit speech.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q03/p1", "position": "Joseph deliberately veiled the identities to spare the condemned man.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir says this spared the other prisoner; al-Biqa'i says each could hope for restoration unless he asked directly; al-Alusi invokes trust in the interpretation and good companionship; Ibn Ashur says the condemned man could grasp his fate gradually."}, {"id": "12:41/q03/p2", "position": "The verse may abbreviate Joseph's direct assignment of each fate.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the verse may condense the original speech in which Joseph named each man's outcome."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q04", "question": "How does the cupbearer's dream yield the timing of his restoration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q04/p1", "position": "Three grape clusters or vine branches mean three more prison days before his return to service.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives three days. Al-Thalabi speaks of three clusters; al-Kalbi in al-Wahidi of a vine with three branches and pressed grapes; al-Tabrisi specifies release on the fourth day. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi take the vine as the king and favorable standing. Ikrima's report in al-Durr describes planting a seed, its growth into clusters, pressing, and serving the king."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q05", "question": "How do the baker's baskets yield the timing of his crucifixion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q05/p1", "position": "Three baskets mean three more days before execution and the birds eating his head.", "reasons": "Al-Thalabi says crucifixion is on the fourth day; al-Kalbi, Ibn al-Sa'ib, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, and al-Alusi link the three baskets to three days. Al-Baghawi says release after three days is followed by crucifixion. Al-Mawardi notes that birds had eaten bread from the dream baskets."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q06", "question": "How is فيسقي read?", "turns_on": "The verb's active or passive morphology and, for the passive, who receives the drink.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q06/p1", "position": "The common active reading derives from saqā: he gives his master wine.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls it the majority reading; al-Samin describes its open yāʾ and derivation from saqā. Al-Durr records Ikrima reciting the active wording."}, {"id": "12:41/q06/p2", "position": "An active reading derives from asqā, with the same drink-serving sense.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report the variant; al-Samin attributes a damma to Ikrima and compares 56:69; al-Alusi also reports it."}, {"id": "12:41/q06/p3", "position": "The passive reading yusqā rabbahu has the master or king given wine.", "reasons": "Ikrima and al-Jahdari are named by Ibn Jinni, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin; Abu Hayyan explicitly identifies the king as recipient. Al-Samin says rabbahu is nominative and notes al-Zamakhshari attributes the reading only to Ikrima. Ibn Jinni sees parallel favorable and punitive passive outcomes. Al-Alusi also reports a passive with riyyihi as a second object."}, {"id": "12:41/q06/p4", "position": "The passive reading means the cupbearer himself is given drink.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari glosses Ikrima's passive as his being given drink to satisfy him; Ibn Atiyya also says he is given wine to drink."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q07", "question": "Do saqā and asqā have the same meaning?", "turns_on": "Whether Arab usage treats the two forms as synonyms or distinguishes direct drinking from provision of water.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q07/p1", "position": "They can both mean giving a person a drink.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls them synonymous; al-Qurtubi reports some linguists' synonymy; Abu Hayyan cites the Lawami author; al-Samin compares the reading at 56:69; al-Alusi allows this shared sense."}, {"id": "12:41/q07/p2", "position": "Saqā gives a drink directly, whereas asqā provides water or irrigation.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj states the distinction; al-Nahhas says most linguists make it, cites Qur'anic form against a poem claiming synonymy, and prefers it. Al-Qurtubi cites al-Nahhas with 77:27; Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi call it the usual distinction."}]}

{"id": "12:41/q11", "question": "What does quḍiya mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q11/p1", "position": "It means completed, settled, or fully executed.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi derives the sense from completing and executing, compares lammā quḍiya and the naming of a qāḍī. Ibn Qutayba traces qaḍā to determination and completion, cites a poem about completing affairs, and explains qāḍī as one who settles disputes; he compares the decreed death in 39:42. Al-Damghani says the prison interpretation is settled or due. Ibn al-Jawzi distinguishes completion in 6:60, 20:114 and 28:28–29, settlement in 6:58, 10:47, 10:54 and 39:69, and irrevocable decree here and in 19:21, 34:14 and 39:42."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q12", "question": "What is the 'matter' that has been decided?", "turns_on": "Whether the inquiry's object is the dreams and their interpretation, the prisoners' eventual fates, or the accusation underlying both cases.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q12/p1", "position": "The men's eventual fates: one will be saved and one killed.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, and al-Samin connect the singular matter to their shared imprisonment or accusation; al-Baydawi says they sought their shared outcome. Al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur take it as what would happen to them. Al-Alusi prefers this as less strained: they asked about dreams in order to learn their fate, so fī is causal; he says inquiry can treat dream and outcome together."}, {"id": "12:41/q12/p2", "position": "The requested interpretation or the dreams as the object of inquiry has been settled.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives the question and answer as finished; Ibn al-Jawzi says the interpretation is settled whether the dreams were true or false. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud and Qatada in al-Wahidi say Joseph only finished the interpretation. Al-Alusi's investigator says a question concerns the dream as an incident, compares the king's request in 12:43, and says 'matter' magnifies obscure dreams; singular matches the prisoners' own wording. Al-Alusi objects that dream and outcome need not be separated this way."}, {"id": "12:41/q12/p3", "position": "The matter is the accusation or crime for which both men were imprisoned.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this view with an omitted term meaning the consequence of that accusation. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan likewise invoke their shared poisoning accusation, while reading the decided matter as its outcome."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q13", "question": "Why is 'matter' singular for two dreams?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular gathers a shared case and fate or echoes the prisoners' phrasing.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q13/p1", "position": "The prisoners share one case or sought one combined outcome.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari identifies the poisoning accusation and the opposed results; al-Baydawi says their inquiry was about the shared case; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin similarly identify the joint accusation and final outcome."}, {"id": "12:41/q13/p2", "position": "The singular follows the prisoners' own singular wording for their dream inquiry.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi's investigator says they asked about the image of an outcome, not their crime or its cause."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q14", "question": "What made Joseph's declaration of a settled outcome certain?", "turns_on": "Whether the declaration reports revealed certainty or merely completion of a probable dream interpretation.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q14/p1", "position": "God revealed or granted Joseph certain knowledge of the men's fates.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer revelation; al-Wahidi prefers it as fitting a prophet, citing fulfillment despite fabricated dreams; al-Tabrisi sees the categorical forecast as revelation of unseen things; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan describe God-given unseen knowledge. Al-Razi allows God to disclose outcomes while Joseph presents dream interpretation. Al-Tabatabai rejects conjecture by the declaration and God's teaching of interpretation. Al-Qurtubi says God fulfilled it to confirm prophethood."}, {"id": "12:41/q14/p2", "position": "As a prophet, Joseph could trust what God caused him to say.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi distinguishes a prophet's certainty from a nonprophet's."}, {"id": "12:41/q14/p3", "position": "He completed the interpretation without guaranteeing the predicted events.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud and Qatada as reported by al-Wahidi take the declaration as the end of the answer. Ibn al-Jawzi offers the same alternative. Al-Razi invokes 12:42's ظن against revealed certainty and allows interpretive judgment without inevitability. Al-Qushayri says even true dream interpretation works by preponderant probability."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q15", "question": "Does interpretation itself make a dream's predicted event binding?", "turns_on": "Whether interpretation normally fixes a dream's fulfillment or Joseph's fulfilled words were a special prophetic confirmation.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q15/p1", "position": "A dream is suspended until interpreted and then follows its first interpretation, even if invented.", "reasons": "Abu Ruzayn's Prophetic report adds that a dream is one forty-sixth of prophecy and should be shared only with a discerning person; Anas reports it follows the first interpreter. Ibn Kathir cites Ahmad through Muawiya ibn Hayda and Abu Ya'la through Anas and extends the rule to invented dreams. Al-Alusi repeats the bird's-wing maxim: once told and interpreted, it falls. Al-Durr's Ibn Masud report says the test dreams' interpretation fixed the outcome."}, {"id": "12:41/q15/p2", "position": "A false interpretation does not bind someone; Joseph's case was exceptional divine confirmation.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi says God made Joseph's interpretation occur to confirm his prophethood. His Qatada report has Umar predict alternating faith and apostasy, ending in unbelief, from a claimed dream of alternating growth and drought; the man then denied dreaming. Al-Qurtubi treats Umar as an exceptional divinely inspired person and cites two further accurate intuitions."}]}
{"id": "12:41/q16", "question": "What did the prisoners say after hearing Joseph's interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether both men invented the dreams, both truly dreamed and later denied it, or only one dreamer lied or recanted.", "positions": [{"id": "12:41/q16/p1", "position": "Both admitted they had fabricated dreams to test Joseph or play with him.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud reports this through al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Thalabi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Durr and al-Alusi; some say they had seen nothing, and Joseph replied the decision stood. Al-Zamakhshari reports the test; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan include it among alternatives. Al-Alusi suggests the cupbearer could have lied to protect his companion."}, {"id": "12:41/q16/p2", "position": "Both had real dreams but denied them after the unwelcome interpretation.", "reasons": "Mujahid says the true predictions had already taken effect when the youths claimed play. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report real dreams followed by denial; al-Razi gives displeasure with the answer as a motive. Al-Suddi reports panic; Ibn Kathir's Ibn Masud report includes their later denial. Al-Baydawi says they accused Joseph of lying."}, {"id": "12:41/q16/p3", "position": "Only the condemned baker denied or invented his dream.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj says the condemned man denied dreaming; al-Mawardi reports his protest that they were playing. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan preserve the only-condemned-man variant; al-Nasafi says the baker denied. An Imami report says the second prisoner admitted inventing his dream; the report of Abu Jafar identifies him as the baker.
